q: Which isotope of uranium is fissile and used as the main fuel in most reactors?
why: U-235 splits readily with slow (thermal) neutrons. U-233 is also fissile but comes from thorium, not natural uranium.

q: What is the blue glow seen in reactor cooling pools called?
why: Charged particles moving faster than light travels in water emit Cherenkov radiation.

q: In what year did Chicago Pile-1 achieve the first self-sustaining chain reaction?
why: CP-1 went critical on December 2, 1942.

q: Who discovered the neutron?
why: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

q: What stops alpha particles?
why: Alpha particles are heavy and highly charged, so paper or the outer layer of skin stops them.

q: What is the half-life of carbon-14, roughly?
why: C-14's half-life is about 5,730 years, which makes it useful for dating organic material.

q: What does a moderator do in a thermal reactor?
why: Moderators like water or graphite slow fast neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission in U-235.

q: Which material is commonly used in control rods?
why: Boron absorbs neutrons strongly. Zirconium is used for fuel cladding because it absorbs very few.

q: Which scientist won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry?
why: Marie Curie won physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

q: Where were natural nuclear reactors found that ran about 2 billion years ago?
why: Uranium deposits at Oklo sustained natural fission reactions roughly 2 billion years ago.

q: What unit measures the biological effect of radiation dose?
why: The sievert accounts for radiation type and tissue sensitivity. The gray is absorbed energy; the becquerel is decays per second.

q: Which fusion reaction do most fusion power designs, including ITER, plan to use?
why: D–T fusion has the highest reaction rate at achievable temperatures.

q: What powers the Voyager probes?
why: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators turn heat from Pu-238 decay into electricity.

q: What was the world's first nuclear-powered submarine?
why: USS Nautilus was launched in 1954.

q: Roughly what percentage of natural uranium is U-235?
why: Natural uranium is about 0.7% U-235. Power reactor fuel is typically enriched to around 3–5%.

q: Which isotope is the most widely used in medical diagnostic imaging?
why: Tc-99m is used in tens of millions of scans each year thanks to its short half-life and clean gamma emission.

q: What do CANDU reactors use as their moderator?
why: Heavy water (D₂O) lets CANDU reactors run on natural, unenriched uranium.

q: Who discovered radioactivity in 1896?
why: Becquerel noticed uranium salts fogging photographic plates.

q: Which element in smoke detectors makes them work?
why: Americium-241 ionizes the air in the detector chamber; smoke disrupts that current.

q: Which experiment revealed that atoms have a small, dense nucleus?
why: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed a few alpha particles bouncing back sharply.

q: What type of radiation needs dense shielding like lead or thick concrete?
why: Gamma rays are high-energy photons with no charge, so they penetrate deeply.

q: Which country's Obninsk plant first supplied nuclear electricity to a grid?
why: Obninsk in the USSR connected to the grid in 1954.

q: What does 'SMR' stand for in nuclear energy?
why: Small modular reactors are designed to be smaller and factory-built.

q: Which element is about 3–4 times more abundant in Earth's crust than uranium and studied as a fuel?
why: Thorium-232 can breed fissile U-233 in a reactor.

q: Who, with Otto Frisch, first explained nuclear fission theoretically in 1939?
why: Meitner and Frisch interpreted Hahn and Strassmann's results as the nucleus splitting.

q: In a pressurized water reactor, why is the primary coolant kept at high pressure?
why: High pressure keeps the water liquid well above 300 °C.

q: What does a Geiger–Müller tube detect?
why: Radiation ionizes the gas inside, triggering the familiar click.

q: About how much energy does one U-235 fission release?
why: Around 200 MeV per fission — millions of times more than a chemical reaction.

q: Which naturally radioactive isotope is found in bananas?
why: Bananas are rich in potassium, a tiny fraction of which is radioactive K-40.

q: What is the average annual natural background radiation dose for a person, roughly?
why: Worldwide averages are around 2.4–3 mSv per year, mostly from radon.
